assessment.nobel_worthiness: Active-matter hydrodynamics supplies a clean, universal account of collective motion far from equilibrium: the Vicsek model shows a flocking transition, Toner-Tu theory shows that long-range order survives in two dimensions through a nonequilibrium hydrodynamic mechanism, and Ramaswamy's work established the hydrodynamics of active fluids and suspensions. It is a clear case of a simple mechanism explaining messy multi-scale behaviour across bacteria, cytoskeleton, flocks and colloids, and it has changed how statistical physics treats driven systems.
assessment.attribution: Vicsek (1995 numerical model), Toner and Tu (1995 continuum theory and its extensions) and Ramaswamy (active-gel and active-suspension hydrodynamics) are the three founding strands. This is a fairly natural trio, though others (e.g. Marchetti, Prost, Julicher, Liverpool) made important contributions and the boundary of the credit is open to dispute.
assessment.maturity: The theory has stood for 25-30 years, is analytically controlled in the Toner-Tu case, and has been tested in experiments on swimmers, vibrated granular media, colloidal rollers and cell layers. Confirmation is broad, though quantitative tests of the exact exponents are still partial. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should centre on flocking (Vicsek, Toner-Tu) or on active gels and fluids (Ramaswamy and others) is open.
Experimental verification of the Toner-Tu scaling exponents is incomplete.
Credit in the wider active-matter community is spread over more than three people.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1984 conformal bootstrap programme for two-dimensional critical systems produced exact critical exponents and operator content for minimal models and a classification framework linking statistical mechanics, string theory and quantum field theory. It is a foundational paper in the sense of containing almost everything that followed: universality classes of 2D critical phenomena, the central charge, and the later bootstrap ideas. Its impact on theory is very deep.
assessment.attribution: Belavin, Polyakov and Zamolodchikov wrote the decisive 1984 paper, so the trio is natural. Contributions of Friedan, Qiu, Shenker, Cardy, Dotsenko, Fateev and Knizhnik are significant for unitarity, modular invariance and Coulomb-gas methods, and may be thought to be underweighted. Polyakov appears on other candidates, which raises no problem in itself.
assessment.maturity: Mathematically mature and widely confirmed against exact lattice solutions and numerics, with experimental checks in 2D critical systems and the Kondo/edge physics context. Recognition is not premature and is arguably late.
uncertainties: Pure theory with limited direct experimental signature; the committee may wish for empirical connection.
Credit boundaries against Cardy, Friedan, Shenker and others.
One laureate is deceased or has uncertain eligibility; I cannot verify the status of each from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned the Hubbard model and other many-body Hamiltonians into controllable laboratory systems. The Jaksch-Zoller proposal and the Greiner-Bloch observation of the superfluid to Mott insulator transition opened a field with quantum gas microscopes, out-of-equilibrium dynamics and synthetic gauge fields. It links my own interests in statistical mechanics, stochastic dynamics and computation in a deep way.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Cirac made the central theoretical proposals (with Jaksch et al. for the Bose-Hubbard lattice); Bloch and Greiner carried out the decisive Mott transition experiment and developed the platforms. The candidate lists four names, so a trio forces a choice; Greiner's contribution is substantial and leaving him out is a real allocation problem. Cirac and Zoller also have a separate candidate entry, which suggests overlap in credit.
assessment.maturity: Over two decades of confirmation by many independent groups; the Mott transition and quantum gas microscopy are standard. The impact on quantum simulation of unresolved problems such as high-Tc physics is still developing, but the experimental techniques are mature.
uncertainties: Selection of three from four names; omitting Greiner is contentious.
Overlap with candidate entries on trapped-ion and atomic quantum computation could split recognition.
Whether quantum simulators have yet solved a problem beyond classical reach is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the 2018 experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened moire materials as a platform for strongly correlated physics. The idea is simple and general, a long-wavelength moire potential that quenches kinetic energy, and has spread to many other van der Waals systems.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the 2011 prediction of the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators (including Cao and Fatemi, who may deserve consideration) made the experimental discovery. Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto earlier identified flat-band physics, an attribution complication. The supplied trio is a sensible theory-plus-experiment pairing.
assessment.maturity: Observation replicated by many groups; the mechanism of superconductivity is still debated and the field is changing quickly. Recognition is timely but possibly early on the superconductivity aspect, while the flat-band and correlated-insulator parts are secure.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity is unsettled.
Credit for early flat-band theory (Lopes dos Santos et al.) and for the experimental co-first authors.
Whether a more stable moire result such as the fractional Chern insulator should be awarded later.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fluctuation theorems give exact, universal relations for entropy production and work in systems driven far from equilibrium, generalising the second law to the level of individual trajectories and linking microscopic reversibility to macroscopic irreversibility. This is the sort of rigorous, simple and general statement I value, and it underlies stochastic thermodynamics, single-molecule experiments and nonequilibrium free-energy methods.
assessment.attribution: Evans, Cohen and Searles (1993 numerical and then analytical statement), Gallavotti and Cohen (1995 chaotic hypothesis) and Jarzynski (1997 equality) are the usual names; Crooks, Kurchan, Lebowitz and Spohn, Seifert and Searles also made decisive contributions. A trio is hard to defend without leaving out Cohen, Searles or Crooks.
assessment.maturity: Verified experimentally in RNA pulling, colloids, and electronic and quantum systems; the theory is mathematically settled and widely used. The impact on practical physics, however, is more conceptual than directly applied.
uncertainties: Genuinely ambiguous allocation of credit among at least six people.
Impact is conceptual; some committee members may weigh applicability differently.
Distinct assumptions (chaotic hypothesis versus Markov/stochastic derivations) are not all settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Liquid-liquid phase separation as an organising principle of intracellular compartments (P granules, nucleoli) connects polymer and soft-matter physics with cell biology. The key idea, that membraneless organelles are liquid-like condensates governed by phase-separation thermodynamics, is simple and general and has reshaped cell biology.
assessment.attribution: Hyman and Brangwynne published the 2009 P-granule paper, with Jülicher providing the physical theory in that work and later on active droplets. The credit is plausible, but whether this is physics rather than biology for the prize, and the contribution of Rosen, Rosen, McKnight and others for related work, are open questions.
assessment.maturity: Broadly replicated, but the physiological relevance of phase separation versus alternative assembly mechanisms is still debated, and in vivo evidence is uneven. The field is young and moving quickly; there is a risk of premature recognition.
uncertainties: Whether the prize falls within physics rather than chemistry or physiology/medicine.
Debate on the in vivo significance of liquid-like behaviour.
Other contributors who could displace one of the three.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect (Kane-Mele, with BHZ) and the experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells created topological insulators as a new class of band structures with protected edge states. It is a clean concept built on a topological invariant, with large impact on condensed matter and later on topological photonics and other fields.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the original theoretical proposal; Molenkamp's group did the 2007 observation, which was based on the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (and Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan for 3D) are not on the supplied list, so the credit is arguably incomplete. Two overlapping topological-insulator candidates suggest that credit is spread.
assessment.maturity: Mature: confirmed in several materials and in 3D, with edge-state transport observed, although some quantized-conductance results are less clean than the theory. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Incomplete credit without Zhang, Bernevig, Hughes, Fu or Hasan.
Competition with the other topological-insulator candidate entries.
Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics realised strong light-matter coupling on a chip and became the basis of superconducting quantum processors and quantum-limited readout. It is a conceptual transfer of cavity QED, with a clean model analysed in a rigorous way, and it has large experimental impact.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf made the 2004 proposal and 2004 experiment; Girvin is absent from the three-name list, which is a credit problem. Recognition of superconducting-circuit quantum physics in 2025 (macroscopic quantum tunnelling) may reduce the room for a further prize in this area.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced across the world and technologically mature; recognition is timely, although the 2025 prize on a neighbouring subject raises the question of priority.
uncertainties: Whether the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits makes a second award in the area unlikely.
Girvin and others missing from the credited list.
My recollection of the 2025 prize details is from memory and is unverified.
